prompt: A frame from a 35mm feature film, full-bleed, 16:9: a wide, high, vertiginous view straight down the stairwell of a five-storey Chicago tenement, 1928, grey morning light falling from a grimy skylight above. In the near foreground at upper left, huge and close, a landlord in a moth-eaten fur collar leans on the banister with his gloved palm turned up and out, waiting. On the landing shelf right beside the lens sits a round glass goldfish bowl, and half the frame is seen through it: the curved water bends the square stairwell into a spiralling funnel, the worn banisters coiling inward like a whirlpool, one orange fish smeared into a long copper streak across it. At the very bottom of the well, five floors down and tiny, the baker, a heavy-set Black man with a shaved head in a sweat-stained vest, climbs with a small envelope in his hand. A bare bulb on each landing gives a pool of sour yellow, and a red-glass night lamp on the third floor stains one coil of the stair crimson. Dry, scuffed treads worn to bare wood, peeling paint, a baby pram, a coal bucket, rope-tied laundry. Grain, deep shadow between the landings. Doors and walls bare of numbers or lettering.
